transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Aisha (PrismBridge Head of Platform), Tom (CTO), Hannah (Infra), Diego (Security)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — can you all hear me okay?
[00:05] Aisha: Yep, sounds good. Thanks for setting this up Maya.
[00:08] Tom: Morning all, or afternoon i guess for some of us. Short intro from our side — i'm Tom, CTO at PrismBridge. Our platform handles routing for retail analytics and we want lower latency for inference calls and better cost predictability.
[00:22] Maya: Awesome — quick intros from our side: Liam is our solutions eng who will go into perf stuff, i'm the AE and i'll handle contract / pilot scope, and we'll make sure security docs get routed to Diego.
[00:34] Liam: Hi all. Quick note: we do hybrid deployments (hosted, dedicated, private VPC), typically customers start with hosted + dedicated reserve for steady qps then move to VPC/private for compliance.
[00:46] Hannah: Two things up front — one, we have strict data residency in EU and some PHI-ish logs for a subset of customers; two, our current inference stack is a mix of self-hosted Triton endpoints and a managed queue system. We want to understand if Redwood can plug in as a drop-in inference backend or if we need adapters.
[01:03] Liam: Totally. Short answer: we provide multiple integration modes. For low-friction POCs we recommend hosted API with a routing policy to your region, but for residency or PHI you'd typically use Redwood Private (VPC) or on-prem bundle; both support customer KMS and audit logs.
[01:19] Diego: On KMS — we use HashiCorp Vault now, must have envelope encryption and HSM-backed keys for some workloads. Can Redwood integrate?
[01:27] Maya: Yes — our Private deploy supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and we can support Vault integrations. We'll follow up with the security whitepaper and a Vault integration pattern doc.
[01:37] Aisha: Good. On performance: our 95th latency target for user-facing features is 120ms end-to-end. Right now the model inference portion is 60–80ms for small prompts, but that spikes. We need consistent tail latency — how do you approach that?
[01:51] Liam: Fair question. Two levers: runtime optimizations (kernel selection, quantized model variants) and serving patterns (continuous batching + prefix/KV caching). For user-facing low-latency we often suggest smaller quantized variants with per-request fast path and prefix cache for repetetive prompts. For tails we use smart routing to fall back to a lower-latency model variant.
[02:10] Tom: When you say smart routing, do you have control plane hooks to route by latency objective? We want traffic split rules in edge cases.
[02:18] Liam: Yes — policy based routing. You can route by region, cost tier, or latency SLO. There're also automatic fallbacks when dedicated capacity is saturated.
[02:27] Aisha: Okay. Cost is another huge thing — our CFO hates surprises. Demoed numbers would help. Do you have per-token estimates for a 7B-13B class model on a dedicated pool?
[02:39] Maya: We'll send a tailored spreadsheet. For back-of-envelope: hosted per-token varies by model family; on dedicated we show unit economics per GPU-hour with batching assumptions. We'll build a cost model for your qps distribution.
[02:50] Hannah: We can share traffic histograms and typical sequence lengths. We'll need to ensure batching won't increase P95 beyond our SLO.
[02:58] Liam: Right. Continuous batching is workload-aware — it prioritizes latency SLOs and will cap batching windows. There's a tradeoff: more batching reduces cost but can add latency. We can tune that per-route.
[03:11] Diego: Security — audit logs, SSO, SAML, and RBAC are must-haves. Also need logs to be write-once for compliance. Can you produce tamper-evident audit trails?
[03:22] Maya: Our Console supports per-request tracing and token-level cost/latency breakdowns. Audit logs are available and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll include SOC2 docs, and we support SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning.
[03:33] Diego: Great. Any certifications? SOC2 Type II is key for us.
[03:36] Maya: Yes, SOC2 Type II — we'll share the attestation and the compliance pack.
[03:40] Aisha: Integration pattern — we have an internal adaptor service (kinda sidecar) that currently shards traffic across Triton clusters. Ideally Redwood would be an alternate backend with minimal code changes. Any SDKs or is it pure REST?
[03:53] Liam: REST first — simple POST generate endpoints. We also have SDKs in Python/Go and plugin examples for common edge proxies. For a more transparent switch, teams use our routing agent that sits in your VPC to route between Triton and Redwood instances.
[04:09] Tom: That routing agent — is it open source? What's the operational surface?
[04:13] Liam: It's a lightweight agent we can run as a k8s DaemonSet. We'll share the repo link. It streams telemetry back to the Redwood Console and can be configured to keep traffic on-prem for the Private deployment.
[04:25] Aisha: POC ask: we want a 3-week bench (synthetic) to validate latency/cost, then an 8-week pilot on a small percentage of production traffic. Is that a typical path?
[04:36] Maya: That's standard. For the bench we provision a small dedicated pool so you're not contending with the hosted tier. Then pilot uses routing rules at 5–10% with canary rollback policies.
[04:46] Tom: Who owns the GPU provisioning during the bench? We need predictable throughput.
[04:50] Liam: For Dedicated we allocate GPU pools with a commit. For bench we usually reserve a time-boxed pool. We provide throughput forecasts by model/seq length for each GPU type.
[04:59] Hannah: We want to run a couple of our internal LLMs — are there restrictions on model types or custom weights?
[05:06] Liam: We onboard custom models. There are tuning steps for kernel selection and quantization; some model formats need conversion but we support the common ONNX/ORT and HF formats. We'll coordinate with your infra team on model packaging.
[05:22] Diego: Regarding data retention, can we control logs retention and ensure PII redaction?
[05:27] Maya: Yes, retention policies are configurable and we have redaction hooks. For Private deployments we can also set retention to zero and keep logs inside your VPC only.
[05:36] Aisha: Any gotchas you typically see with partners?
[05:39] Liam: Two big ones: engineers underestimate tail noise from long inputs which breaks batching assumptions, and RBAC/SSO integration takes longer than expected if the IDP team isn't looped in early.
[05:49] Tom: Good to know. On the commercial side, our procurement timeline is next quarter. We'll need pricing and a standard enterprise addendum for data residency.
[05:59] Maya: We'll put together pilot pricing and an enterprise addendum draft. Also include a runbook for private deployment onboarding.
[06:07] Aisha: Ok, last question — fallback strategies if a region loses capacity. We don't want user visible errors.
[06:13] Liam: We support automatic fallback to compatible model variants, regional routing to alternative clusters, and circuit-breaker policies. You can configure silent degrade (shorter context, smaller model) or failover.
[06:24] Diego: Will the audit logs indicate fallback events?
[06:27] Maya: Yes, all routing events and overrides are logged with request ids.
[06:32] Maya: Great. To recap: Redwood to share SOC2 & Vault+KMS pattern docs, an initial cost/latency spreadsheet tailored to PrismBridge traffic, and the agent repo + sample k8s configs. PrismBridge to send histograms, sample prompts, and the IDP contact for SSO. We'll schedule an SE deep-dive next week focused on perf.
[06:54] Tom: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[06:58] Aisha: Thanks — talk soon.

End of transcript.
